cells.tense: The shapes you draw are carrying weight you never stand around to collect.
cells.ask: Name one standard you hold that nobody handed you. Say it once, quietly, then leave it standing.
cells.core: You draw the frame of a thing and then step back and let it hold. That's not control. It's real architecture, and it keeps working after you've left the room. People move inside the pattern you set and organize themselves around it, and you read that as them managing fine on their own. They're not. The shape did that, and you made the shape. What tends to go missing is the plain acknowledgment, even to yourself, that the thing didn't assemble itself. When you name one standard you actually hold, you learn which structures are earning their keep and which you're propping up out of habit. Both are worth knowing. The first ones get to stay.
cells.sheetLine: You build the frame and forget the frame was yours.
cells.verb: building a thing so it holds once the making of it is done
cells.place: the desk where a shape gets drawn before anyone else has to live in it

cells.tense: You're drawing the frame around outcomes that haven't arrived yet and may never.
cells.ask: Take one plan and let a piece of it land differently than you drew it. Don't correct it. Leave it where it fell.
cells.core: You're mapping the next quarter and the next conversation before either has happened, and the drawing is getting tighter than anything real could fit into. Loosen one corner and the fear says the whole thing slides. So you brace by design, and the place you're actually in becomes a rehearsal for a better one later. That's the cost: today's attention goes to a room no one has entered. Letting one part come out unlike the drawing isn't wrecking anything. It shows you what the structure can carry without you standing over it, and it draws the line between design and dread. Some of what you call planning is just holding the future still so it can't surprise you. It surprises you anyway.

cells.tense: The shape is finished, and you're still standing at the desk where it was drawn.
cells.ask: Take the most finished thing you have and put it in front of one person today. Send it as it is.
cells.core: You can build the structure. It's still there, complete, holding. What stopped is the standing in the room where it gets used. A showing once didn't go the way you wanted, and the desk became the safer place to stay. So you keep making and keep not arriving. The work on your screen is the version nobody else got, and from where you're standing it looks unfinished. It isn't. Put something in front of a person and watch what it does. That's the cut of seeing that returns you to the room — not the missing pieces, the ones already standing. You're allowed back in. The structure you built will hold you being there.

cells.tense: Your hand is on the frame and you're describing it as the frame holding itself.
cells.ask: Say 'I made this' about one structure people already move inside. Say it plainly, no qualifiers.
cells.core: You point at the schedule, the team, the system — at anything except the shape you drew. The meeting agenda is yours. The project's frame is yours. You just talk about it like it assembled itself. That story costs more than credit. It stops you from changing what you built, because you can't revise something you won't admit you made. Set it down simply: this one came from you. That's not ego. It's the earlier, simpler version of the same act — the moment the line first started, before it got complicated enough to feel like something that just happens. Say the small true thing about the thing in front of you, and the structure becomes something you can pick back up.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that their structures already reach further than they think — a reading taken and it didn't hold easily would leave that line exposed, so I am not leaning on it. The reader could reasonably say the design work is shared, not carried by them alone, so each cell speaks to the making of the shape rather than sole authorship of it. The asks stand if the read is wrong: naming a standard, letting a draft read as drawn, holding one meeting at two items, saying 'I built this' are all small acts that cost nothing and teach something. The sentence that serves me more than them is the last one, so I have done what I can to write it to them.
